analysis.one_liner: Tightens court oversight and public disclosure of deals that let corporations escape criminal conviction.
analysis.headline: The bill would require courts, not prosecutors alone, to approve deals letting corporations avoid criminal convictions, and would ban paid deals to drop prosecutions; it has only been referred to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets a common practice: when a company is caught breaking federal law, prosecutors often let it avoid a criminal conviction by signing a deferred or non-prosecution agreement promising fines, reforms, and better behavior. The bill would require a federal judge to approve any such deal, confirm it compensates victims and deters repeat offenses, and ban companies that caused deaths or injuries, laundered money, or were repeat offenders from getting these deals at all. It would also ban paying money in exchange for prosecutors dropping a case, force the Justice Department to publish the terms of all these agreements going back to 1993, and create a new Office of Corporate Enforcement to monitor compliance. The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people harmed by corporate misconduct benefit: victims of corporate offenses would get the right to confer with prosecutors before a deal is struck and to be heard by a judge before it is approved. The public gains transparency, because every deferred and non-prosecution agreement's text, fines, and monitor contracts would be posted publicly, and repeat corporate offenders could no longer buy their way out with a second deal. Taxpayers also gain from an annual report to Congress and a new DOJ office tracking whether companies actually comply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of corporate crime and the public

how_it_helps.text: A federal judge would have to approve any deferred prosecution agreement and confirm it serves the public interest, that penalties are enough to compensate victims and deter repeat offenses, and that victims were consulted before the deal was offered.

Companies that caused deaths or serious injuries, committed money laundering or trafficking offenses, or had already been convicted of or signed agreements over similar offenses would be barred from getting deferred prosecution deals at all.
Paying money in exchange for prosecutors dropping a corporate case would be banned, and any such deal would be void and unenforceable.
The Justice Department would have to post the text, terms, fines, monitor contracts, and prior convictions of these deals on its public website, covering agreements going back to 1993.

A new Office of Corporate Enforcement would monitor compliance with the deals and report violations, and the Attorney General would report annually to Congress on every agreement, including instances of non-compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations and their executives pay if it passes: they would face court-approved deals with tougher terms, higher fines set to actually compensate victims and deter repeat offenses, a ban on paying to make investigations go away, public exposure of every settlement term, and a complete bar on deferred deals for repeat offenders or companies whose offenses killed or injured people. Corporate defense firms that negotiate these deals would also see a less flexible process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations and their defense lawyers

drawbacks.text: Banning non-prosecution agreements outright and adding court approval removes flexibility prosecutors use to resolve difficult corporate cases; in some cases, a negotiated resolution may be the only realistic path when proof at trial is uncertain, and the bill could push more cases toward civil settlements instead of criminal accountability.

Court review of every deferred prosecution agreement, including mandatory hearings where victims are heard, would add time and cost to resolving corporate cases, and companies facing those costs may pass them on to consumers or shareholders.

The bill leaves the Justice Department itself in charge of writing the new guidance and staffing the new enforcement office, so its strength in practice would depend on how seriously future administrations implement it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefits for ordinary people are accountability and information: courts, victims, and the public would see and shape the deals that let large companies avoid criminal convictions, and serial violators would lose access to those deals altogether. The costs are real but narrower: prosecutors would lose a fast, flexible tool for resolving hard-to-prove corporate cases, which could slow some resolutions or shift more cases to civil settlements, and compliance costs for large companies are likely passed to consumers and shareholders at the margins. On balance the bill imposes a modest, targeted constraint on prosecutorial convenience in exchange for greater transparency and a stronger deterrent against repeat corporate offenders.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the House and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no amendments, and no floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 15, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action has been taken since the referral: no committee vote, no hearing listed, and no floor consideration.
The bill has 9 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large corporations and their defense lawyers are better off, because the current system of privately negotiated deals that let companies avoid convictions remains untouched. Ordinary people gain nothing because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations keeping quiet settlement options

for.name: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Prosecution Reform Act to add court oversight, victim rights, and public disclosure to corporate prosecution deals.

for.name: Reps. Norton, Ross, Tlaib, Johnson of Georgia, Evans, Deluzio, and Dean
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill at introduction.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on May 15, 2026; has taken no further action on it to date.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors and the sponsor are Democrats, with no Republican support in the record so far.

industries.note: The bill would make it harder to buy a way out of a criminal case, bar repeat offenders from deferred prosecution entirely, and expose the full terms of their deals to the public. Fines and monitor costs could rise, and shareholders and consumers may bear some of those costs.

A core product of large defense practices is negotiating quiet resolutions with the Justice Department. Mandatory court approval, published terms, and a ban on paid non-prosecution deals would shrink that market and make negotiations more adversarial.

Court-reviewed agreements and published monitor contracts could raise the bar for who gets monitor work and on what terms, but the new Office of Corporate Enforcement and closer judicial oversight would also create structured demand for monitoring services.

The bill locks in the deferred-prosecution model as the permanent, regulated channel for resolving corporate crime, rather than eliminating it. It would also rename the Justice Department's white collar crime grant program to cover cyber and financial crime, redirecting that program's framing.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since its referral with no hearings or markup, and carries no Republican cosponsors in a chamber where majority support is needed to reach the floor. Most bills at this stage with one-party sponsorship and no committee action die quietly when the Congress ends, so it is unlikely to advance unless the committee schedules it or it picks up bipartisan backing.
